say: In February twenty-ten, South Koreans were reported tapping iPhones with snack sausages, to keep their gloves on.
show: In February 2010, South Koreans were reported tapping iPhones with *snack sausages,* to keep [their gloves on.]

say: Because your phone ignores a wool glove, however hard you press. So what is your screen feeling for?
show: Because your phone ignores a *wool glove,* however hard you press. So what is your screen [feeling for?]

say: Under the glass sits an invisible grid of see-through wires: rows one way, columns the other.
show: Under the glass sits an *invisible grid* of see-through wires: rows one way, [columns the other.]

say: The phone sends tiny electric pulses along the rows, and measures what reaches each column, many times a second.
show: The phone sends tiny *electric pulses* along the rows, and measures what reaches each column, [many times a second.]

say: Your finger is mostly salty water, so charge moves through it. Bring it close, and it draws away part of the signal at the crossings under it.
show: Your finger is mostly *salty water,* so charge moves through it. Bring it close, and it draws away part of the signal [at the crossings under it.]

say: By comparing neighbouring crossings, the phone finds the centre of your touch, even between wires.
show: By comparing neighbouring crossings, the phone finds the *centre of your touch,* [even between wires.]

say: A wool glove or a fingernail barely changes the signal. Water can, so a wet screen sometimes taps by itself.
show: A wool glove or a fingernail *barely changes* the signal. Water can, so a wet screen sometimes [taps by itself.]

say: And the sausage? Salty, moist meat changes that signal too. Your screen never knew it was your finger. It only feels a change in the signal, and a sausage can fake that.
